subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

choices: An organism or virus that causes disease
Any microorganism living in the body
A protein that triggers antibody production
A white blood cell that destroys bacteria
items.note: Pathogens include viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists. An antigen is the molecule recognised by the immune system.

items.stem: Which is part of the body's first line of defence?
choices: Antibodies made by plasma cells
Skin and mucous membranes
Phagocytes engulfing bacteria
Memory B cells in lymph nodes
items.note: Physical/chemical barriers stop entry. Phagocytes are innate but act after entry; antibodies belong to the adaptive response.

choices: Viruses but not bacteria
Both bacteria and viruses
Neither bacteria nor viruses
Bacteria but not viruses
items.note: Antibiotics target bacterial processes (e.g. cell wall, 70S ribosomes). Viruses use host cell machinery, so they are not affected.

items.stem: During blood clotting, the role of thrombin is to:
choices: Release clotting factors from platelets
Make antibodies against the invading pathogen
Convert soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin
Dissolve the clot once the damaged wound has healed
items.note: Clotting factors from platelets and damaged tissue activate thrombin, which converts fibrinogen → fibrin threads that trap cells.

items.stem: Phagocytes are part of the innate immune system because they:
choices: Make antibodies specific to one antigen
Respond in the same non-specific way to any pathogen
Remember specific pathogens from earlier infections of the body
Only respond after vaccination
items.note: Innate = non-specific and unchanged by exposure. Adaptive = specific, with memory.

items.stem: Activation of a B lymphocyte to divide into plasma cells requires:
choices: Binding of any antigen to any receptor on its surface
Engulfing a pathogen by phagocytosis and then digesting it completely
Exposure to an antibiotic that kills the pathogen
Binding of its antigen and signals from an activated helper T cell
items.note: Both antigen binding and helper T cell activation are needed; clonal selection then produces many plasma cells.

items.stem: Memory cells give long-lasting immunity because they:
choices: Persist and respond quickly with many antibodies on re-infection
Produce large amounts of antibody continuously throughout life
Destroy pathogens by phagocytosis as soon as they enter
Stop pathogens from crossing the skin barrier
items.note: On second exposure memory cells divide rapidly, giving a faster, larger secondary response.

choices: Spread only between plants
Are caused only by bacteria
Pass from other animals to humans
Cannot ever be passed on by contact
items.note: Examples include tuberculosis, rabies, COVID-19. Many new infectious diseases are zoonotic.

items.stem: HIV reduces the ability to fight infections mainly because it:
choices: Infects red blood cells and so reduces the oxygen carried to tissues
Destroys platelets, so blood does not clot
Directly kills all antibodies in the blood plasma
Infects and destroys helper T cells, so fewer antibodies are made
items.note: Without helper T cells, B cells are not activated; AIDS follows, with opportunistic infections.

items.stem: Herd immunity protects unvaccinated people because:
choices: They receive antibodies from vaccinated people nearby
Vaccinated people kill pathogens in the air around them
So many people are immune that the pathogen cannot spread easily
The pathogen mutates to a harmless form in vaccinated people
items.note: When a large proportion are immune, chains of transmission are broken, protecting those who cannot be vaccinated.

items.stem: Antibiotic resistance in a bacterial population increases mainly because:
choices: Resistant variants survive treatment and reproduce, so their alleles become common
Bacteria develop resistance in response to the antibiotic
Antibiotics cause mutations that make bacteria resistant
Patients become immune to the antibiotic after using it many times, so it stops working
items.note: Natural selection: random mutations give resistance; the antibiotic kills susceptible cells; resistant ones survive and multiply.

markscheme: Vaccine contains antigens (weakened/inactivated pathogen, or mRNA coding for an antigen) (1)
Triggers a primary immune response: specific B and T cells activated, antibodies made (1)
Faster, larger secondary response if the real pathogen infects (1)
items.tactic: Chain of events: antigen → response → memory → protection.

items.stem: Outline the role of antibodies in defence against pathogens.
markscheme: Antibodies bind to specific antigens on the pathogen (1)
They make pathogens clump together (agglutination) / neutralise toxins (1)
They mark pathogens for phagocytes (opsonisation) / activate complement (1)
items.tactic: Give the binding step, then at least two consequences.

items.stem: Compare the primary and secondary immune responses.
markscheme: Both produce specific antibodies against the antigen (1)
Secondary produces more antibody / higher peak (1)
Secondary is due to memory cells from the primary response (1)
items.tactic: Compare graphs: lag time, peak, duration, plus the reason.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) Cases of an invented infectious disease per 100 000 people in four regions, with vaccination coverage: Region A 95% coverage, 2 cases; B 85%, 15 cases; C 70%, 120 cases; D 50%, 410 cases.
(a) Describe the relationship between coverage and cases. (b) Calculate how many times more cases occur in D than in A. (c) Explain why cases rise sharply below about 85% coverage. (d) Suggest one other factor that could explain differences between regions.
markscheme: (a) Higher coverage, fewer cases (negative correlation), not linear (1)
(c) Below a threshold there are enough susceptible people for the pathogen to keep spreading / herd immunity is lost (1)
Each infected person can infect more than one other (1)
(d) e.g. population density, healthcare access, hygiene, travel, age structure (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
